newsitem.title: USA: Jury asked to find Simpson responsible for murders.
newsitem.headline: Jury asked to find Simpson responsible for murders.

text.p: An attorney dramatically pointed the finger of blame at O.J. Simpson on Tuesday, telling jurors in his civil trial: "There's a killer in this courtroom."

In an impassioned final summation, Daniel Petrocelli, the plaintiffs' lead lawyer, said the voices of Simpson's ex-wife and her friend were speaking "from the grave" and accusing the former American football star of being their killer.
Calling Simpson "a guilty man, a man with no remorse, a man with no conscience," Petrocelli exhorted jurors to find him responsible for the June 1994 murders.
He contended Simpson offered no explanation for the mass of blood and DNA evidence linking him to the crime and has "lied and lied and lied about every aspect of this case."

Simpson, who was acquitted on Oct. 3, 1995, in the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman, is battling a wrongful-death civil lawsuit brought by the victims' families. If he loses, he cannot be punished with jail but he could be forced to pay millions of dollars in damages.
Closing arguments were expected to spread over two days, with the case going to the jury as early as Thursday.
Describing Simpson as a spoiled celebrity with a superiority complex, Petrocelli accused him of weaving a web of lies when he took the witness stand earlier in the trial.

Most dubious, Petrocelli said, was Simpson's denial that he ever owned the kind of Bruno Magli shoes that left bloody prints at the murder scene -- testimony that was countered by at least 30 photographs apparently showing him wearing the Italian designer shoes at a 1993 football game.
And Petrocelli contended that contrary to the claims of Simpson's defence team, there was no proof any evidence was planted to frame him.
But the most dramatic moment came when Petrocelli asked jurors to think of the victims when they decide if Simpson is responsible for the murders.

"The critical pieces of evidence are ... the voices of Nicole and Ron speaking to us from the grave, telling us, telling all of you, that there is a killer in this courtroom," Petrocelli said, pointing at Simpson.
Continuing to jab his finger in Simpson's direction, he declared: "That is the man who confronted them, attacked them and killed them, the defendant, Orenthal (James) Simpson."
Petrocelli said the victims "in their last struggling moments to stay alive provided us with the key evidence necessary to identify their killer."

He said the glove and knit cap that the attacker left at the murder scene, the fingernail marks and cuts he alleged they left on Simpson's hand and the bloody shoeprints that led away from the bodies were ample proof of Simpson's guilt.

Unlike the criminal trial, which required "proof beyond a reasonable doubt," the plaintiffs in the civil trial will prevail if they can prove there is a 50.1 percent probability -- a "preponderance of the evidence" -- that Simpson committed the murders. And only nine of the 12 jurors' votes are required for a judgment for or against Simpson.

In terms of its racial breakdown, the civil court jury bears little resemblance to the mostly black panel that acquitted Simpson in his criminal trial. It is made up of seven women and five men, among them nine whites, one Hispanic, one black and one Asian-black.

Many legal analysts consider it a crucial factor. Simpson is black; the murder victims were white. National polls show that blacks are more likely to view Simpson as innocent while most whites believe he got away with murder.
